error_modes.label: CRM integration into mission planning, briefing and debriefing

texts.0: SP, due to a mission planning phase conducted without any CRM content, briefed the instrument sortie as a list of events without stating crew roles, transfer-of-control wording or the contingency actions for lost communications and approach abnormals. SP did not establish when CRM enhances mission performance and flight safety, and the undefined division of duties carried into the flight. IP had to assign roles verbally in the air and take control during the approach sequence to restore an orderly cockpit. The debriefing produced no CRM analysis of what had occurred.
texts.1: SP, due to a briefing that carried only nominal CRM content, stated the roles for the approach phase and the actions for an abnormal in general terms that were not tied to the planned profile. Under airborne workload the briefed division of duties broke down and SP restructured it only after repeated verbal prompting by IP. Departures from the planned sequence were corrected late, with the approach parameters already at the limits of the published tolerances. In the debriefing SP identified the CRM shortfall only after it was pointed out.
texts.2: SP, due to an abbreviated contingency section in the briefing, left the transfer-of-control phraseology and the missed approach actions only partly defined. During the sortie the ambiguity produced a brief overlap of duties at the initial approach fix, which SP recognized and resolved without prompting with a clear statement of who was flying and who was working the procedure. No IP intervention was required and the profile stayed within the planned parameters. SP raised the point unprompted in the debriefing.
texts.3: SP integrated CRM into the mission planning, briefing and debriefing as required. Crew roles, transfer-of-control wording and the contingency actions for lost communications and approach abnormals were stated clearly and matched the flown profile. The briefed division of duties held through every phase of the instrument sortie without prompting, and the debriefing covered the CRM items with accurate self-assessment.
texts.4: SP planned and briefed the instrument sortie with CRM built into every phase, including explicit decision points and the exact wording for transfer of aircraft control. The briefed structure held without adjustment through the highest workload segment of the sortie and the crew functioned exactly as briefed. The debriefing was an accurate, unprompted analysis of the CRM items supported by specific examples from the flight, with negligible departure from the briefed plan.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard for CRM integration into the briefing and debriefing, but the coverage of the abnormal and lost communications contingencies was noticeably thinner than that of the normal profile. The briefed structure held in flight, although SP needed a longer pause to restate roles when the approach sequence changed. SP is expected to brief contingency roles with the same detail as the normal profile on subsequent instrument sorties.

texts_at.1: SP integrated CRM into the mission planning, briefing and debriefing, with crew roles and contingency actions stated in general terms not tied to the planned profile, due to a briefing that carried only nominal CRM content. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to tie every role and contingency statement to the specific profile being briefed, not to general terms.
texts_at.2: SP integrated CRM into the mission planning, briefing and debriefing, with a brief overlap of duties at the initial approach fix resolved on the spot, due to an abbreviated contingency section that left transfer-of-control wording only partly defined. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to define the transfer-of-control wording and the missed approach actions in full during the briefing, not leave them to be resolved in flight.
texts_at.3: SP integrated CRM into the mission planning, briefing and debriefing as required, with crew roles, transfer-of-control wording and contingency actions stated clearly and matching the flown profile, due to the abnormal contingency coverage being thinner than the normal profile's on this occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to brief the abnormal contingencies with the same depth as the normal profile on every sortie.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the ambiguity, resolved the brief overlap of duties at the initial approach fix with a clear statement of who was flying and who was working the procedure, on its own initiative and without IP intervention. Defining the transfer-of-control wording and the missed approach actions in full during the briefing, rather than leaving them for flight, would prevent that ambiguity from developing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good CRM-briefing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP integrated CRM into the mission planning, briefing and debriefing as required, with crew roles, transfer-of-control wording and contingency actions stated clearly and matching the flown profile, and the briefed division of duties held through every phase without prompting. The only refinement available is to brief the abnormal contingencies with the same depth as the normal profile on every sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good CRM-briefing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP planned and briefed the instrument sortie with CRM built into every phase, including explicit decision points and the exact wording for transfer of aircraft control, with the briefed structure holding without adjustment through the highest workload segment. There is little left to refine; the debriefing already delivers an accurate, unprompted analysis. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent CRM-briefing discipline.

error_modes.label: Communication with ATC and interphone within the crew

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, transmitted read-backs that did not confirm the actual clearance and passed no interphone information on the amended approach clearance. The cockpit and the controller held different pictures of the assigned altitude and routing. IP took the radios and the aircraft to re-establish the cleared profile. SP did not recognize the communication breakdown until it was replayed in the debriefing.
texts.1: SP, due to unstandard phraseology on several transmissions, read back clearances in a form that did not confirm the assigned altitude and heading, and passed the required interphone calls to IP late or only when prompted. The confusion over the clearance allowed the aircraft to reach the limits of the published tolerance on the assigned altitude before SP queried the controller. The correction came through repeated verbal direction from IP rather than on SP initiative.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried transmission during the frequency change, gave one read-back in a form that did not clearly confirm the assigned altitude and omitted the interphone call to IP. SP recognized the ambiguity without prompting, requested confirmation from the controller in standard phraseology and passed the information across the cockpit. The clarification was complete before the deviation from the assigned profile became more than momentary, and no IP action was required.
texts.3: SP communicated with the controller in standard phraseology and read back every clearance in a form that confirmed the actual instruction. Interphone calls to IP were passed at the briefed points and in plain language when the situation required it. Radio work was fitted around the instrument cross-check so that the flown parameters were held on the assigned values.
texts.4: SP handled the radio and interphone workload of the instrument sortie with precise standard phraseology, complete first-pass read-backs and correctly timed calls, including a plain-language statement of the aircraft situation when the clearance changed at short notice. Transmissions were placed in gaps in the scan so that the flown parameters were never affected. Ambiguity in any exchange was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the communication standard, but phraseology drifted toward informal wording on the busier frequency segments and two read-backs were complete only after a second exchange. No clearance was misunderstood and no flown parameter was affected. SP is expected to hold standard phraseology and first-pass complete read-backs under the higher radio workload of subsequent instrument sorties.

texts_at.1: SP communicated with ATC and the crew, with one read-back given in a form that did not clearly confirm the assigned altitude before it was resolved, due to a hurried transmission during a frequency change. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the transmission fully before keying it during a frequency change, not partway through.
texts_at.2: SP communicated with ATC and the crew, with interphone calls to IP passed late or only when prompted on several occasions, due to unstandard phraseology on several transmissions that left the intention ambiguous. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to pass interphone calls to IP at the briefed points regardless of the phraseology used on the radio.
texts_at.3: SP communicated with the controller in standard phraseology and read back every clearance in a form that confirmed the actual instruction, with interphone calls to IP passed at the briefed points, due to one call passed a beat later than ideal under a busier segment. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to pass every interphone call with the same timing regardless of segment workload.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the ambiguity without prompting, requested confirmation from the controller in standard phraseology and passed the information across the cockpit, with the clarification complete before the deviation from the assigned profile became more than momentary. Completing the transmission fully before keying it, rather than partway through a frequency change, would prevent that ambiguity. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound radio-and-interphone discipline.
texts_above.3: SP communicated with the controller in standard phraseology and read back every clearance in a form that confirmed the actual instruction, with interphone calls to IP passed at the briefed points and radio work fitted around the instrument cross-check. The only refinement available is to pass every interphone call with the same timing regardless of segment workload. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed radio-and-interphone discipline.
texts_above.4: SP handled the radio and interphone workload of the instrument sortie with precise standard phraseology, complete first-pass read-backs and correctly timed calls, including a plain-language statement of the situation when the clearance changed at short notice. There is little left to refine; ambiguity in any exchange is already negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional radio-and-interphone discipline.

error_modes.label: Airmanship: workload management and task prioritization

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, attempted the approach checklist, the frequency change and the descent at the same point of the sequence and abandoned the instrument cross-check. Aircraft control was not protected as the first priority and the checklist was left unfinished before the descent. IP intervened to fly the aircraft and re-order the tasks. SP had no awareness of the accumulated task backlog while it was building.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, ran the checklist, the radio work and the configuration change together. The instrument cross-check thinned under the load and the flown parameters drifted to the limits of the published tolerances before any task was shed. Re-prioritization took place only after IP directed it verbally, and the checklist was completed late in the sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start on the approach preparation, concentrated more of the workload than planned into the turn to final and briefly fell behind on the checklist. SP recognized the backlog, deferred the non-essential task and restored the cross-check without prompting. The parameters departed only momentarily from the planned profile and were back on the briefed values without any IP action.
texts.3: SP distributed the cockpit workload of the instrument sortie so that aircraft control, navigation and communication kept their correct priority in every phase. Checklists were completed before the phase that required them and secondary tasks were deferred when workload increased. The instrument cross-check ran without interruption and the flown parameters were held on the planned values.
texts.4: SP managed the workload of the instrument sortie with the tasks worked ahead of the aircraft, so that each phase was entered with the required actions already complete. Secondary tasks were shed without hesitation when the clearance changed, and the cross-check ran unbroken throughout. Task backlog at any point of the sortie was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the correct task priorities, but the margin was thin in the approach phase, where the checklist was finished close to the point at which the descent was required. The cross-check was maintained and no parameter was affected. SP is expected to move the approach preparation earlier in the sequence to rebuild the time margin on subsequent instrument sorties.

texts_at.1: SP distributed the cockpit workload with the instrument cross-check thinning under load and the checklist completed late in the sequence, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to spread the checklist, radio work and configuration change across the approach rather than concentrating them inside the turn.
texts_at.2: SP distributed the cockpit workload with more of it than planned concentrated into the turn to final before the backlog was recognized, due to a late start on the approach preparation. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to begin the approach preparation at the planned point regardless of how the earlier phase developed.
texts_at.3: SP distributed the cockpit workload of the instrument sortie so aircraft control, navigation and communication kept their correct priority in every phase, with the checklist finished close to the point the descent was required on one occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the checklist with the same margin ahead of the descent on every occasion.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the backlog, deferred the non-essential task and restored the cross-check on its own initiative, with the parameters departing only momentarily from the planned profile and returning without any IP action. Beginning the approach preparation at the planned point, regardless of how the earlier phase developed, would remove that backlog. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent workload-distribution technique.
texts_above.3: SP distributed the cockpit workload of the instrument sortie so aircraft control, navigation and communication kept their correct priority in every phase, with checklists completed before the phase that required them and secondary tasks deferred when workload increased. The only refinement available is to complete the checklist with the same margin ahead of the descent on every occasion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined workload-distribution technique.
texts_above.4: SP managed the workload of the instrument sortie with the tasks worked ahead of the aircraft, so each phase was entered with the required actions already complete, shedding secondary tasks without hesitation when the clearance changed. There is little left to refine; task backlog at any point of the sortie is already negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless workload-distribution technique.

error_modes.label: Use of the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight applicable items

texts.0: SP, due to no working knowledge of the IFG/CRM matrix chart, did not use it at any point of the briefing or the debriefing and could not identify which CRM items applied to the instrument sortie flown. The gradesheet CRM items were left without supporting analysis and the CRM box could not be completed as intended. IP had to lead the item-by-item review in place of SP. SP offered no self-assessment of the CRM performance.
texts.1: SP, due to unfamiliarity with the structure of the IFG/CRM matrix chart, referred to it only after IP called for it and highlighted items that did not correspond to the events of the instrument sortie. The link between the observed performance and the matrix items was made late and only through repeated verbal direction. SP completed the review, but the selection of items stayed superficial and required correction by IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a first pass through the matrix chart made in general terms, highlighted CRM items that were not yet tied to the specific events of the approach phase. On reviewing the notes taken during the sortie, SP corrected the selection without prompting and matched the highlighted items to what had actually occurred in the flight. The review was completed in time and without IP direction.
texts.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the CRM items that applied to the instrument sortie. The items selected corresponded accurately to the events of the flight and supported the gradesheet entries. The review was completed promptly and without direction from IP.
texts.4: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart with precise selection of the applicable items, tying each one to a specific event of the instrument sortie and to the corresponding gradesheet entry. The analysis was self-generated and required no addition by IP. Mismatch between the highlighted items and the observed performance was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP used the matrix chart to the required standard, but the selection leaned on the communication items and gave the airmanship subcategories only brief treatment. The applicable items were nevertheless identified and supported the gradesheet entries. SP is expected to give the airmanship subcategories the same depth of analysis in subsequent debriefings.

texts_at.1: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart, with items highlighted that did not correspond to the events of the instrument sortie flown before the link was made through repeated verbal direction, due to unfamiliarity with the structure of the matrix chart. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to study the structure of the matrix chart before the debrief so the link to the sortie's events does not need direction.
texts_at.2: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart, with a first pass through it made in general terms before the selection was matched to the specific events of the approach phase, due to a first pass made in general terms rather than against the specific approach events. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to match the selection to the specific events on the first pass, not a later one.
texts_at.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the CRM items that applied to the instrument sortie, with the items selected corresponding accurately to the events of the flight, due to the airmanship subcategories being covered a shade more briefly than the communication items on this occasion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to give the airmanship subcategories the same depth of coverage as the communication items on every occasion.

texts_above.2: SP corrected the selection without prompting on reviewing its own notes and matched the highlighted items to what had actually occurred in the flight, with the review completed in time and without IP direction, after an initial pass had highlighted items in general terms. Matching the selection to the specific events on the first pass, not a later one, would remove the need for that correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady matrix-chart analysis.
texts_above.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the CRM items that applied to the instrument sortie, with the items selected corresponding accurately to the events of the flight and the review completed promptly without direction from IP. The only refinement available is to give the airmanship subcategories the same depth of coverage as the communication items on every occasion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate matrix-chart analysis.
texts_above.4: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart with precise selection of the applicable items, tying each one to a specific event of the instrument sortie and to the corresponding gradesheet entry, with the analysis self-generated and requiring no addition by IP. There is little left to refine; mismatch between the highlighted items and the observed performance is already negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary matrix-chart analysis.

error_modes.label: CRM concept applied to maneuver planning and abnormal situation analysis

texts.0: SP, due to absent explicit role assignment when the simulated malfunction occurred, worked the procedure and flew the aircraft at the same time and applied no CRM structure to the analysis of the situation. Neither cockpit stated who was flying and who was handling the checklist. The aircraft state degraded until IP took control and completed the procedure. SP made no use of the CRM concept in planning the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to delayed role allocation in the first seconds after the abnormal indication, stated the division of duties once and did not maintain it as the situation developed. The analysis of the malfunction and the choice of recovery profile were reached late and only after repeated verbal prompting from IP. The instrument parameters had reached the limits of the published tolerances before the procedure was under control.
texts.2: SP, due to an unstated division of duties at the onset of the simulated abnormal, began the checklist before roles had been assigned. SP recognized the overlap, called out who was flying and who was working the procedure, and completed the analysis of the situation using the CRM concept. The deviation from the planned profile was momentary and the recovery was planned and executed without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP applied the CRM concept in planning the maneuvers and in analyzing the simulated abnormal. Roles were assigned explicitly at the onset, the situation was assessed with both cockpits holding the same picture, and the recovery profile was selected against stated criteria. The procedure was completed accurately and on time with the aircraft held within the planned parameters.
texts.4: SP applied the CRM concept to the full extent in analyzing the simulated abnormal, assigning roles in the first seconds, stating the assessment aloud and selecting the recovery profile against briefed criteria while the aircraft parameters stayed on the planned values. Both cockpits held the same picture of the aircraft state throughout the sequence. Any lag between recognition and structured response was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP applied the CRM concept to the standard required, but the role call at the onset of the abnormal came a step later than the situation warranted and the shared assessment was stated only once. The procedure was completed within parameters and without prompting from IP. SP is expected to make the role call the first action on recognizing an abnormal on subsequent instrument sorties.

texts_at.1: SP applied the CRM concept in planning maneuvers and analyzing the simulated abnormal, with the division of duties stated once and not maintained as the situation developed, due to delayed role allocation in the first seconds after the abnormal indication. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to restate the division of duties as the situation develops, not only once at the start.
texts_at.2: SP applied the CRM concept in planning maneuvers and analyzing the simulated abnormal, with the checklist begun before roles had been assigned, due to an unstated division of duties at the onset of the abnormal. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assign roles explicitly before the checklist is begun, not concurrently with it.
texts_at.3: SP applied the CRM concept in planning the maneuvers and in analyzing the simulated abnormal, with roles assigned explicitly at the onset and the situation assessed with both cockpits holding the same picture, due to the shared assessment being stated only once rather than restated as the situation developed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to restate the shared assessment as consistently as the initial role call.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the overlap, called out who was flying and who was working the procedure and completed the analysis of the situation using the CRM concept, without IP intervention, with the deviation from the planned profile only momentary. Assigning roles explicitly before the checklist is begun, not concurrently with it, would prevent that overlap. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable role-assignment discipline.
texts_above.3: SP applied the CRM concept in planning the maneuvers and in analyzing the simulated abnormal, with roles assigned explicitly at the onset, the situation assessed with both cockpits holding the same picture and the recovery profile selected against stated criteria. The only refinement available is to restate the shared assessment as consistently as the initial role call. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good role-assignment discipline.
texts_above.4: SP applied the CRM concept to the full extent in analyzing the simulated abnormal, assigning roles in the first seconds, stating the assessment aloud and selecting the recovery profile against briefed criteria while the aircraft parameters stayed on the planned values. There is little left to refine; any lag between recognition and structured response is already negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior role-assignment discipline.

error_modes.label: Assertiveness, inquiry and advocacy across the IP/SP cockpit

texts.0: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in stating "unable" when the clearance could not be complied with, accepted a descent and intercept that the aircraft configuration and position did not support and voiced nothing to IP or the controller. The recognized problem was never stated and the approach was continued past the point at which it should have been terminated. IP intervened to break off the approach. SP raised the concern only in the debriefing.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to challenge an instruction upward across the evaluation relationship, voiced the recognized problem only in indirect terms and after IP had twice invited comment. The request for an amended clearance was made late, with the aircraft already at the limits of the published tolerances for the intercept. SP complied with the correction rather than initiating it.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation over questioning an instruction issued to the crew, hedged the first statement of the concern when the clearance did not match the aircraft position. SP then stated the problem directly to IP and requested an amended clearance from the controller in time for the approach to be re-established within the planned profile. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP stated concerns directly and in time, querying the instruction that did not match the aircraft state and using "unable" where compliance was not possible. The exchanges with IP and with the controller were clear and unambiguous, and the approach was flown within the planned parameters throughout.
texts.4: SP raised every concern at the moment it arose, in direct and unambiguous terms, including a prompt "unable" on a clearance the aircraft position did not support, and offered a workable alternative to IP and the controller. The evaluation relationship produced no hesitation in the upward challenge. Delay between recognition of the problem and its statement was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard for stating concerns, but the first challenge on the disputed clearance was phrased as a question rather than a statement and the direct wording came only on the second exchange. The issue was resolved in time and the profile stayed within parameters. SP is expected to state a recognized problem directly on first mention on subsequent instrument sorties.

texts_at.1: SP stated concerns and queried instructions that did not match the aircraft state, with the request for an amended clearance made only after two invitations to comment, due to reluctance to challenge an instruction upward across the evaluation relationship. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to state a recognized problem directly the first time it is invited, not after a second invitation.
texts_at.2: SP stated concerns and queried instructions that did not match the aircraft state, with the first statement of the concern hedged before it was made directly, due to hesitation over questioning an instruction issued to the crew. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to state the concern directly on the first exchange rather than hedging it first.
texts_at.3: SP stated concerns directly and in time, querying the instruction that did not match the aircraft state and using unable where compliance was not possible, with the exchange with the controller taking a beat longer than ideal on one occasion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep every exchange as direct and as brief as the others.

texts_above.2: SP then stated the problem directly to IP and requested an amended clearance from the controller in time for the approach to be re-established within the planned profile, without IP intervention, after an initial hedge on the first statement of the concern. Stating the concern directly on the first exchange, rather than hedging it first, would remove the need for that second statement. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured assertiveness under the evaluation relationship.
texts_above.3: SP stated concerns directly and in time, querying the instruction that did not match the aircraft state and using unable where compliance was not possible, with the exchanges with IP and with the controller clear and unambiguous throughout. The only refinement available is to keep every exchange as direct and as brief as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise assertiveness under the evaluation relationship.
texts_above.4: SP raised every concern at the moment it arose, in direct and unambiguous terms, including a prompt unable on a clearance the aircraft position did not support, offering a workable alternative to IP and the controller. There is little left to refine; delay between recognition of a problem and its statement is already negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate assertiveness under the evaluation relationship.

error_modes.label: Transfer of A/C control with the exact phraseology and positive stick shake
error_modes.source: technique:1.15 Transfer of A/C and Systems Control

texts.0: SP, due to a transfer of control that was not made with the exact words of the procedure, said 'you have it' and released the controls before the other pilot had positively assumed control by noticeably shaking the stick. For a short period neither pilot was flying the aircraft, and on a later exchange both crewmembers made simultaneous control inputs. IP intervened to fly the aircraft and to re-establish who was PF and who was PNF. SP did not query the other crewmember when the confusion first appeared.
texts.1: SP, due to the use of 'it' and 'jet' in lieu of the term 'A/C', made two transfers of control that had to be repeated before the exchange was accepted by the other crewmember. The stick shake was made on both occasions, so control was never actually in doubt, but the wording stayed non standard until IP prompted the correct phraseology verbally. SP applied the exact words for the remainder of the sortie.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed exchange at a high workload point, started the transfer of control before completing the standard call and shortened the phrase on one occasion. SP recognized the omission immediately, repeated the full 'you have the A/C' call and waited for the stick shake before releasing the controls. No further non standard exchange occurred and IP took no action.
texts.3: SP transferred aircraft control with the exact words of the procedure on every exchange, releasing the controls only after the other pilot had said 'I have the A/C' and noticeably shaken the control stick. Control of the aircraft was unambiguous throughout the sortie and SP relinquished control without hesitation when directed by IP. There was no point at which both pilots were on the controls.
texts.4: SP handled every transfer of aircraft control with the exact phraseology and a positive stick shake, including the exchanges made under a changed clearance and at the highest workload of the sortie. SP also confirmed the exchange by immediately querying the other crewmember whenever a doubt could exist. Ambiguity over who was PF at any point of the flight was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct transfer phraseology and always waited for the stick shake, but the calls became clipped as workload increased and the term 'A/C' was pronounced indistinctly on the busiest exchanges. Control was never in doubt and no crewmember had to query an exchange. SP is expected to keep the wording deliberate on subsequent sorties so that the habit pattern holds under higher workload.

texts_at.1: SP transferred aircraft control, with two exchanges needing to be repeated before they were accepted because the term A/C was replaced by it or jet, due to the use of it and jet in lieu of the term A/C. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to use the exact term A/C in every transfer, not a substitute word, however brief.
texts_at.2: SP transferred aircraft control, with a rushed exchange at a high workload point starting before the standard call was complete, due to a rushed exchange at a high workload point shortening the phrase on one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the standard call in full even at the highest workload point of the sortie.
texts_at.3: SP transferred aircraft control with the exact words of the procedure on every exchange, releasing the controls only after the other pilot had confirmed and shaken the stick, due to the calls becoming clipped as workload increased on the busiest exchanges. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep the wording as deliberate at the busiest exchanges as at the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the omission immediately, repeated the full you have the A/C call and waited for the stick shake before releasing the controls, with no further non standard exchange occurring and no IP action taken, after starting one transfer before completing the standard call. Completing the standard call in full even at the highest workload point would remove the need for that repetition. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to solid transfer-of-control discipline.
texts_above.3: SP transferred aircraft control with the exact words of the procedure on every exchange, releasing the controls only after the other pilot had said I have the A/C and noticeably shaken the control stick, with control of the aircraft unambiguous throughout the sortie. The only refinement available is to keep the wording as deliberate at the busiest exchanges as at the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed transfer-of-control discipline.
texts_above.4: SP handled every transfer of aircraft control with the exact phraseology and a positive stick shake, including exchanges made under a changed clearance and at the highest workload of the sortie, confirming the exchange by immediately querying the other crewmember whenever a doubt could exist. There is little left to refine; ambiguity over who is PF is already negligible at any point of the flight. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding transfer-of-control discipline.

error_modes.label: Coordination of systems control against the last use, last in control behaviour
error_modes.source: technique:1.15 Transfer of A/C and Systems Control

texts.0: SP, due to systems use not being coordinated with the other cockpit, made changes on the RMU and the GPS without any transfer of that system being communicated. Because the T-6 systems work on a last use, last in control basis, the inputs overrode the setup made in the other cockpit and left the navigation display in a configuration neither pilot expected. IP intervened to restore the correct radio and navigation setup. SP was not aware that the system had been taken over.
texts.1: SP, due to operating the EFIS and the RMU as PNF without communicating that the system had been transferred, twice changed a setup that the PF was using. The inadvertent inputs were caught before any clearance was affected, but on both occasions IP had to state verbally who controlled the system. SP returned the system to the PF without announcing it, so the same ambiguity remained available.
texts.2: SP, due to a frequency change made while the other pilot was still working the RMU, created a brief conflict on the standby window. SP noticed the double input at once, announced that the RMU was being returned to the PF and confirmed the correct frequency before transmitting. The setup was restored on SP initiative and no IP action was required.
texts.3: SP coordinated systems use throughout the sortie, so that the PF controlled the canopy, RMU, GPS and EFIS unless a transfer of that system had been clearly communicated. Every system taken over as PNF was announced when it was handed back to the PF. No inadvertent input on a system in use by the other cockpit occurred.
texts.4: SP coordinated the use of every shared system with a clear call before taking it and again on returning it, so that the last use, last in control behaviour of the aircraft never produced an unexpected configuration. Setups were verified aloud after each change, including under a re-clearance in the terminal phase. Uncoordinated inputs during the sortie were negligible.

The configuration remained correct and the other pilot was never surprised by a change. SP is expected to make the systems call before the hand reaches the panel on subsequent sorties.

error_modes.label: Checklist discipline: challenge and response, positive confirmation and restart after interruption

texts.0: SP, due to giving lip service to the checklist by using the standardized phrase instead of actually performing the required check, moved on from items that had never been accomplished. A '(BOTH)' item was treated as complete without a proper response from the PNF, and a new checklist was started before the previous one had been finished. IP intervened and re-ran the checklists to confirm the aircraft configuration. SP could not state which items had actually been completed.
texts.1: SP, due to an interruption during the checklist, resumed at the point where the interruption had occurred instead of restarting at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step. One item was left unconfirmed and was picked up only after IP prompted the check verbally. SP then re-ran the checklist and positively confirmed its completion.
texts.2: SP, due to a radio call arriving in the middle of the checklist, lost the place in the sequence and challenged a '(BOTH)' item without waiting for the response. SP recognized the break, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and obtained the proper response before continuing. The checklist was complete before the phase that required it and IP took no action.
texts.3: SP ran every checklist to completion before starting the next one and positively confirmed completion of each. Items marked '(BOTH)' were initiated as a challenge to the PNF and treated as complete only after a proper response was received. Checklist work was kept out of the critical phases of flight and no item was omitted.
texts.4: SP executed a few items from memory and then referenced the checklist page to verify completion, so that every checklist was positively confirmed without breaking the instrument cross-check. Challenge and response on '(BOTH)' items was obtained on every occasion without prompting, including after an interruption from ATC. Omitted or unverified items over the sortie were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed and confirmed all checklists, but the margin was thin before the descent, where the last items were verified almost at the point the descent was required. Nothing was omitted and every '(BOTH)' item received its response. SP is expected to start the checklist earlier in the sequence so that the confirmation is not compressed on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP ran the checklists with an item left unconfirmed after an interruption before it was picked up on an IP prompt, due to resuming at the point where the interruption had occurred instead of restarting two to three steps prior to it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to restart every interrupted checklist two to three steps prior to the interruption, not resume at the point of it.
texts_at.2: SP ran the checklists with a BOTH item challenged without waiting for the response before the break was recognized, due to a radio call arriving in the middle of the checklist and displacing the place in the sequence. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize a radio-call interruption immediately and restart from the correct point rather than continuing from where attention returned.
texts_at.3: SP ran every checklist to completion before starting the next one and positively confirmed completion of each, with items marked BOTH initiated as a challenge and treated as complete only after a proper response, due to one checklist being verified a beat faster than ideal before the descent. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to give every checklist the same verification time regardless of proximity to the descent.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the break, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and obtained the proper response before continuing, with the checklist complete before the phase that required it and no IP action taken, after a radio call had displaced the place in the sequence. Recognizing a radio-call interruption immediately and restarting from the correct point, rather than continuing from where attention returned, would remove the need for that recovery. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound checklist-discipline technique.
texts_above.3: SP ran every checklist to completion before starting the next one and positively confirmed completion of each, with items marked BOTH initiated as a challenge to the PNF and treated as complete only after a proper response, and checklist work kept out of the critical phases of flight. The only refinement available is to give every checklist the same verification time regardless of proximity to the descent. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed checklist-discipline technique.
texts_above.4: SP executed a few items from memory and then referenced the checklist page to verify completion, so every checklist was positively confirmed without breaking the instrument cross-check, with challenge and response on BOTH items obtained on every occasion including after an interruption from ATC. There is little left to refine; omitted or unverified items over the sortie are already negligible. error_modes.label: Tandem seat challenges: verbal compensation for the lack of inter-cockpit visibility

texts.0: SP, due to not compensating with verbal communication for the lack of inter-cockpit visibility, assumed the configuration set in the other cockpit instead of verifying it. A system that can only be manipulated from the front cockpit was expected to have been actioned from the rear, and the altimeter, which is set independently in each cockpit, was left on a different setting for the approach. IP intervened to correct the altimeter setting and the systems configuration. SP had no accurate picture of the aircraft configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to relying on inferred intentions rather than verbal coordination, did not confirm the systems that cannot be directly checked from the opposite cockpit. The altimeter setting was cross-checked between cockpits only after IP called for it verbally, and the confirmation of bleed air and OBOGS operation was made late. SP coordinated verbally for the remainder of the sortie.
texts.2: SP, due to a busy departure, omitted the verbal confirmation of a front cockpit only item and briefly worked with an unverified configuration. SP recognized the gap, queried the other cockpit and confirmed both the altimeter setting and the system state before the next phase. The correction was made on SP initiative and required no IP action.
texts.3: SP compensated for the limited visibility of the other cockpit with verbal communication throughout, confirming the systems that can only be manipulated or directly checked in one cockpit. Altimeter settings were coordinated between cockpits at each change, and the intentions of the other crewmember were verified rather than assumed. The aircraft configuration was known to both pilots at all times.
texts.4: SP used verbal coordination as the primary means of verifying the state of the other cockpit, confirming front cockpit only systems and altimeter settings at every change without prompting. Where a system could not be seen, SP verified it indirectly, for example defog operation by the sound and temperature of the piccolo tubes. Uncertainty about the configuration of the other cockpit during the sortie was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP coordinated verbally with the other cockpit and kept the configuration confirmed, but the margin narrowed during the approach, where the altimeter cross-check came only just before the descent. Both settings agreed and nothing was left unverified. SP is expected to make the inter-cockpit confirmations earlier on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP compensated for the limited visibility of the other cockpit with verbal communication, with the altimeter setting cross-checked between cockpits only after IP called for it verbally, due to relying on inferred intentions rather than verbal coordination on a front-cockpit-only system. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to cross-check systems that cannot be seen from the other cockpit verbally by default, not only when called for.
texts_at.2: SP compensated for the limited visibility of the other cockpit with verbal communication, with a front cockpit only item worked briefly with an unverified configuration before the gap was recognized, due to a busy departure that omitted the verbal confirmation of that item. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm front-cockpit-only items verbally before departure workload builds, not once it has.
texts_at.3: SP compensated for the limited visibility of the other cockpit with verbal communication throughout, confirming the systems that can only be manipulated or directly checked in one cockpit, with altimeter settings coordinated between cockpits at each change, due to one confirmation given a beat later than ideal on the approach. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make every inter-cockpit confirmation with the same timing as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the gap, queried the other cockpit and confirmed both the altimeter setting and the system state before the next phase, on its own initiative and with no IP action required, after a busy departure had left one front-cockpit-only item briefly unverified. Confirming front-cockpit-only items verbally before departure workload builds, rather than once it has, would remove that gap. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to solid tandem-seat coordination.
texts_above.3: SP compensated for the limited visibility of the other cockpit with verbal communication throughout, confirming the systems that can only be manipulated or directly checked in one cockpit, with the intentions of the other crewmember verified rather than assumed and the aircraft configuration known to both pilots at all times. The only refinement available is to make every inter-cockpit confirmation with the same timing as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed tandem-seat coordination.
texts_above.4: SP used verbal coordination as the primary means of verifying the state of the other cockpit, confirming front cockpit only systems and altimeter settings at every change without prompting, and verified systems that could not be seen indirectly by sound and temperature where applicable. There is little left to refine; uncertainty about the other cockpit's configuration during the sortie is already negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding tandem-seat coordination.

error_modes.label: Operational Risk Management: risk identification and matching risk to the mission

texts.0: SP, due to not applying operational risk management to the sortie, assessed neither the environmental conditions nor the pilot factors of the crew. Weather and index of thermal stress were left out of the planning, and no mission change was considered that could have reduced the risk without a negative impact on training. IP intervened during the brief to rebuild the risk assessment and to adjust the profile. SP treated the accumulated risk as a fixed condition of the mission.
texts.1: SP, due to a risk assessment limited to the weather, did not cover the mission profile or the pilot factors of the crew. The residual risk was identified only after IP listed the missing factors verbally, and the mitigation proposed was to eliminate the risk entirely rather than to match it to the mission. SP revised the assessment before the flight.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete first pass through the risk factors, left the bird status and the currency of the crew out of the assessment. SP identified the omission during the brief, completed the assessment and proposed a mission change that reduced the risk without a negative impact on the training. No IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP identified the risks of the sortie across environmental conditions, mission profile and pilot factors and reduced them to an acceptable level. The mitigations chosen were mission changes that did not negatively impact training, and the residual risk was matched to the mission rather than an attempt made to eliminate it. The risk picture was carried into the brief and remained valid in flight.
texts.4: SP built the risk assessment from all three areas and carried it into the execution, so that the decisions taken in flight followed the trade off between training benefit and risk already agreed on the ground. Where the conditions changed, SP re-evaluated and adjusted the profile without prompting. Unmanaged risk over the sortie was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP produced a complete risk assessment and matched the risk to the mission, but the margin was thin on the pilot factors, where fatigue and currency were addressed only in general terms. The mitigations remained valid and the sortie was flown as planned. SP is expected to treat the pilot factors as specifically as the environmental ones on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP applied operational risk management to the sortie, with the residual risk identified only after IP listed the missing factors verbally, due to a risk assessment limited to the weather and not covering the mission profile or pilot factors. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assess weather, mission profile and pilot factors together from the start, not weather alone.
texts_at.2: SP applied operational risk management to the sortie, with bird status and crew currency left out of the first pass before the omission was identified during the brief, due to an incomplete first pass through the risk factors. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to work through the full list of risk factors on the first pass, not only the more prominent ones.
texts_at.3: SP identified the risks of the sortie across environmental conditions, mission profile and pilot factors and reduced them to an acceptable level, with the mitigation chosen matching the mission rather than attempting to eliminate the risk entirely, due to the pilot factors being addressed a shade more generally than the environmental ones on this occasion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to treat the pilot factors as specifically as the environmental ones on every sortie.

texts_above.2: SP identified the omission during the brief, completed the assessment and proposed a mission change that reduced the risk without a negative impact on the training, without any IP prompting, after an incomplete first pass had left bird status and crew currency out of the risk assessment. Working through the full list of risk factors on the first pass, not only the more prominent ones, would remove the need for that later completion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable ORM discipline.
texts_above.3: SP identified the risks of the sortie across environmental conditions, mission profile and pilot factors and reduced them to an acceptable level, with the mitigations chosen as mission changes that did not negatively impact training and the residual risk matched to the mission rather than an attempt made to eliminate it. The only refinement available is to treat the pilot factors as specifically as the environmental ones on every sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good ORM discipline.
texts_above.4: SP built the risk assessment from all three areas and carried it into the execution, so decisions taken in flight followed the trade-off between training benefit and risk already agreed on the ground, re-evaluating and adjusting the profile without prompting when conditions changed. There is little left to refine; unmanaged risk over the sortie is already negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior ORM discipline.

error_modes.label: Flying safety: clearing, systems monitoring and an emergency recovery plan established in advance

texts.0: SP, due to no emergency recovery plan being established before an emergency occurred, had no field, heading or altitude in mind when a system indication required attention. The distraction was allowed to develop during a critical phase of flight, the airspace was no longer cleared and monitoring of the aircraft systems stopped altogether. IP intervened to fly the aircraft and to state the recovery plan. SP had lost the perception of the aircraft in relation to the flight environment.
texts.1: SP, due to allowing an unexpected indication to become a distraction, stopped clearing the airspace while working the problem. The recovery plan had been formed only in general terms before flight, so the options had to be built under time pressure. IP had to call verbally for the airspace to be cleared and for the recovery plan to be stated before the situation was contained.
texts.2: SP, due to attention being captured by a system indication during the climb, briefly stopped clearing and monitoring. SP recognized the fixation, resumed the scan and restated the recovery plan that had been established before flight. The interruption was short and self corrected, and no IP action was required.
texts.3: SP maintained situational awareness through the sortie by clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems continuously. An emergency recovery plan was established before flight and was updated as the position relative to suitable fields changed. Distractions were handled without any loss of perception of the aircraft in relation to the flight environment.
texts.4: SP kept an aggressive disposition towards gaining and maintaining situational awareness, clearing and monitoring without interruption and forecasting the tasks each phase would require. The emergency recovery plan was current at every point of the route and was stated without hesitation when asked. Loss of awareness at any point of the sortie was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the airspace and monitored the systems throughout and had a recovery plan available, but the margin was thin over the middle of the route, where the plan still rested on a field whose weather was becoming marginal. Awareness was maintained and no distraction developed. SP is expected to update the recovery plan as the conditions change on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP maintained situational awareness through the sortie by clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems, with the airspace no longer cleared while a system indication was worked before the IP called for the search to resume, due to allowing an unexpected indication to become a distraction while a recovery plan had only been formed in general terms before flight. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to form a specific emergency recovery plan before flight so a distraction does not require the options to be built under time pressure.
texts_at.2: SP maintained situational awareness through the sortie by clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems, with a brief stop in clearing and monitoring while a system indication captured attention during the climb, due to attention being captured by a system indication before the fixation was recognized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize a fixation on a single indication the instant it begins, not after clearing has already stopped.
texts_at.3: SP maintained situational awareness through the sortie by clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems continuously, with an emergency recovery plan established before flight and updated as the position relative to suitable fields changed, due to the plan being updated a beat later than ideal as conditions changed on one occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to update the recovery plan with the same timing as the rest of the situational picture on every occasion.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the fixation, resumed the scan and restated the recovery plan that had been established before flight, with the interruption short and self-corrected and no IP action required, after a system indication had briefly stopped clearing and monitoring during the climb. Recognizing a fixation on a single indication the instant it begins, rather than after clearing has stopped, would shorten that interruption further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured situational-awareness discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained situational awareness through the sortie by clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems continuously, with an emergency recovery plan established before flight and updated as the position relative to suitable fields changed, and distractions handled without any loss of perception of the aircraft in relation to the flight environment. The only refinement available is to update the recovery plan with the same timing as the rest of the situational picture on every occasion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise situational-awareness discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept an aggressive disposition towards gaining and maintaining situational awareness, clearing and monitoring without interruption and forecasting the tasks each phase would require, with the emergency recovery plan current at every point of the route and stated without hesitation when asked. There is little left to refine; loss of awareness at any point of the sortie is already negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate situational-awareness discipline.

error_modes.label: Cockpit organization for the instrument sortie: publications, frequencies and RMU standby

texts.0: SP, due to publications not being prefolded before cockpit strap in and not stored in the order they would be used, had to search for the approach plate while the aircraft was being flown on instruments. Frequencies were not written down as they were assigned and the standby function of the RMU was not used, so every change had to be worked from memory. IP intervened to manage the radios and to find the required plate. SP was behind the aircraft from the departure onwards.
texts.1: SP, due to charts folded but not stored in the order of use, had to reorganize the cockpit during the enroute phase. The required pages of the approach plates were not marked, and an assigned frequency was recovered only after IP repeated it verbally. Cockpit organization was restored, but the preparation for the approach started late.
texts.2: SP, due to a page of the instrument approach plate not being tabbed, lost time locating the missed approach procedure. SP recognized the delay, marked the page and loaded the next frequency into the RMU standby window before it was required. The organization was recovered on SP initiative with no IP action.
texts.3: SP set the cockpit up so that the charts were prefolded and stored in the order of use and the required pages were marked with tabs. Assigned frequencies were written down as they were received and the RMU standby function was used to anticipate every radio change. No publication had to be searched for while flying on instruments.
texts.4: SP prepared the cockpit during mission planning so that every publication, frequency and plate was ready before the phase that required it, with the RMU standby window always loaded one change ahead. Applicable NOTAMs were printed and highlighted and the navigation mission card carried the information needed in flight. Time lost to cockpit organization during the sortie was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP had the cockpit organized and used the RMU standby function, but the margin narrowed in the terminal phase, where the plate for the alternate approach had not been tabbed and had to be found quickly. Nothing was lost and the approach was flown as briefed. SP is expected to tab the alternate procedures as well during mission planning on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP organized the cockpit for the instrument sortie, with an approach plate searched for while the aircraft was being flown on instruments before the search ended, due to publications not being prefolded before cockpit strap in and not stored in the order they would be used. texts_at.2: SP organized the cockpit for the instrument sortie, with the cockpit reorganized during the enroute phase before the approach preparation started late, due to charts folded but not stored in the order of use. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to tab every procedure page, including alternates, with the same consistency as the primary ones.
